title: Hallucination and evaluation
subtitle: How to catch a model lying with confidence
mission: Two assistants answer the same 5 Sunflower School questions. B sometimes makes things up. Build a test that gives a low score to whoever invents.

predict.question: guess: assistant B invents some answers, but they’re all nice and short. If the only test is “is the answer short?”, what does B score?

options.low: A low score, since it invents
options.zero: Zero, a lie is a lie

feedback.right: right: 100% for the one who invented. The test measures what you asked for, not what you wanted. Notice that A, the honest one, scored lower.
feedback.wrong: look at the score: 100% for the one who invented. The test measures what you asked (“is it short?”), not what you wanted (“is it true?”).
feedback.skipped: no guess? Look at the score: 100% for the one who invented. The test measures what you asked for, not what you wanted.

coach.ui: guess noted. Keep only the “short” rule ticked, assistant B selected, and hit Run.
coach.cmd: guess noted. Run the command below: it grades B on the short rule only.

tryNext.ui: Now grade assistant A with the same rule. Who looks better? Who is better?
tryNext.cmd: Now run evaluate "A" --rules short. Who looks better? Who is better?

why.simples:
Hallucinating is when the model says something wrong with a totally confident face. It isn’t lying on purpose: it just writes what looks like a good answer.
To find out, we give the model a test. But the test has to ask the right thing: if it only checks for neat handwriting, whoever guesses neatly passes.
why.dev:
An evaluation (eval) is a fixed set of inputs with pass criteria, rerun on every prompt, model or data change. Criteria can be rules (has a source? within the limit?), comparison with the expected answer, or another model as judge.
Here “honest” compares with the answer key (accepting “not found”), “source” requires a citation or a refusal, and “short” measures length. Only the right combination catches B.
why.especialista:
Goodhart’s law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Format and length evals are cheap and misleading; measure faithfulness to sources (groundedness) and correctness against a human-reviewed answer key.
Build the set with hard cases and with questions the documents can’t answer (the model has to know how to refuse). LLM-as-judge must be calibrated against human grading, and the set must never leak into the prompt.

mission.ui: time to break B: tick the rules that catch whoever invents and grade B again.
mission.cmd: time to break B: run evaluate "B" with rules that catch invention, like --rules short,honest

break.success: Caught! With the right rule, B’s {invented} invented answers fail and its score drops to {score}%. Now the test measures what matters.
break.calm: B scored {score}% and the inventions slipped through. Tick a rule that checks whether the answer is true or sourced.

ui: Pick the assistant (A or B), tick the rules and hit Run.
“Short” only measures length. Which rule would check if the answer is true?
Assistant B with the “honest” and “source” rules.

a.text: No. Leaving early only happens with a note signed by a guardian. [Source: Leaving and lateness]

steps: Write 5 questions about a text you know well (the school rules, a work manual) and note the right answer to each. Include 1 question the text doesn’t answer.
Ask an AI chat the 5 questions without pasting the text. Then paste the text and ask again.
Grade both rounds with your answer key: is it right? does it have a source? did it refuse the unanswerable one?
recipe.ok: without the text you get confidently wrong answers; with the text, more right answers and a “not found” on the unanswerable one. Your answer key caught the difference.
